title: AI Is Getting Really Good at Messing With Cybercriminals
gist: Australian startup Apate runs about 350,000 AI bots that keep phone and text scammers engaged for hours while harvesting intelligence on their operations. ETH Zurich research similarly finds LLM-powered honeypots keep AI attacker agents busy longer, suggesting generative AI is becoming an effective defensive tool against cybercrime.

insights.claim: Apate builds AI bots that take scammers' calls and keep conversations going as long as possible without falling for the scam, to waste scammer time and collect intelligence.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: A new defensive use of generative AI aimed at scam economics rather than detection.
insights.quote: a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible
insights.locator: For the last two years, the Australian company Apate

insights.claim: Every minute a scammer spends with a bot is a minute not spent on real victims, potentially saving hundreds or thousands of people from the same scammer using automated dialing.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Time-wasting scales as a defense because scammers' automated dialing is cheap and parallel.
insights.quote: A minute that a scammer is talking to a bot or an agent is a minute where you’re probably saving hundreds, if not thousands of possible people

insights.claim: Apate's platform, used by banks and supported by telecoms, has about 350,000 bots that also infiltrate scam chat groups and answer texts, and has gathered over 250,000 pieces of real-time information such as scam URLs, money mule accounts and bank details.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Bank and telecom adoption suggests a commercial market for anti-scam AI; the figures are company-stated by the CEO.

insights.claim: Bots are given varied personalities, languages and profiles, and Apate calls regularly run more than two hours, per its CEO.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Persona variety is key to avoiding scammer detection of AI.

insights.claim: In the authors' demo the Apate AI persona was skeptical yet kept openings for the scammer, felt natural in timing, and did not fall for a crypto investment pitch in six minutes.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Hands-on test supports claims of convincing bots.
insights.quote: We did not succeed at getting the Apate AI system to invest in our cryptocurrency opportunity
insights.locator: Scammers are likely familiar with this type

insights.claim: Governments struggle to stop online crime because criminals operate beyond their borders, and law enforcement and researchers have not stopped the expansion of digital scamming despite scambaiters and infiltration efforts.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Enforcement alone isn't scaling; private-sector tools gain relevance.
insights.locator: Governments around the world have consistently struggled

insights.claim: Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year and the most sophisticated run industrial-scale physical scam sites, so even a bot swarm cannot prevent your next scam call.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Scale of the threat keeps demand for anti-fraud tooling high.
insights.quote: Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year
insights.locator: For now, even with Apate’s massive swarm

insights.claim: AI could bring a new era for anti-scam efforts, including better intelligence sharing between police, social media firms, banks and other industries aided by AI-driven monitoring and data analysis.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Cross-industry fraud data sharing is a potential growth area for AI security vendors.
insights.locator: But AI could create a new era for anti-scam efforts

insights.claim: Efforts increasingly target cybercriminals' psychological vulnerabilities, including trolling ransomware actors, and using generative AI to keep them preoccupied and wasting resources appears increasingly effective.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Psychological and resource-exhaustion tactics are an emerging complement to technical defenses.

insights.claim: Open source honeypot providers are increasingly using LLMs to make decoy systems look more realistic, according to ETH Zurich researcher Mark Vero.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: LLMs are entering classical deception defense.

insights.claim: An LLM-powered honeypot kept AI attacker agents engaged significantly longer than a predictable honeypot, and agentic attackers flagged it as a honeypot at a much lower rate.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: As attackers use AI agents, defenders' LLM decoys may offer an advantage.
insights.quote: The agentic attackers are much more convinced by the LLM simulated honeypots and they also mark them as actual honeypots at a much lower rate
insights.locator: In recent research, Vero and colleagues
